3 ft through the roof · 2 ft above roof within 10 ft

steps: Clearances to combustibles
Check stove (B, D, F) and pipe (A, C, E) clearances for single- or double-wall connector against the p. 9 drawing. Alcoves need double-wall pipe and at least 51" wide × 72" tall.
Site & structure

NFI-certified installer recommended. Never a sleeping room. Keep floor, wall and ceiling/roof structure intact; never cut a load-bearing wall or engineered truss. The stove is heavy: lift with a helper.

NFI-certified installer recommended. Never a sleeping room. Keep the structural integrity of the floor, walls and ceiling/roof; add bracing if required and never cut a load-bearing wall or engineered truss. The stove is heavy: get help and use proper lifting techniques.

Check local building or fire officials for restrictions and inspection requirements. Choose a central location in the main living area; uninsulated basements and garages are inefficient spots.
Floor protection

Non-combustible, under the stove, 6" to the sides (G, to the top plate) and 16" to the front (H, to the face). Type 1 ember protection, no R-value. Through-wall: 2" either side of the horizontal connector.
Assemble the stove

Uncrate; each part ships boxed with its own instructions. Lay the stove on its back, fit the ash pan kit (optional) and legs or pedestal kit, set it upright, then the catalyst and flame diffuser, door and blower (optional).
Chimney & connector

UL-103HT all-fuel chimney or NFPA 211 lined masonry, minimum 6", not shared with another appliance. Connector: 24ga. single wall black pipe or listed double wall (recommended); 3 screws per joint, including 3 at the stove.
Chimney height
Through the roof at least 3 feet and 2 feet above any part of the roof within 10 feet; at least 14 feet stove top to cap, more with offsets (see Min. flue height).
All-fuel chimney

Follow the chimney maker's manual; don't mix brands or use damaged parts. Fit supports, braces, shielding, firestops and an attic insulation shield; never run connector pipe through an attic, closet, wall, floor or ceiling.

Follow the chimney maker's installation manual; the chimney must meet UL-103HT. Don't mix brands of chimney parts and don't use damaged parts. Install supports, braces, shielding and firestops to the chimney maker's recommendations, and an insulation shield in the attic so no insulation touches the chimney. Never pass connector pipe through an attic, closet, wall, floor or ceiling.

Examples of 103 HT systems: DuraTech (DuraVent), Excel (ICC Chimney), Ultra Temp (Selkirk), Temp/Guard (Metal-Fab). Many chimney systems require a 2" air space around the pipe. On a metal roof in a snowy region, consider snow breaks or diverters.
Mobile homes
KA OA 1 outside air kit and double wall connector required. Ground the stove to the home's metal frame with 8-gauge wire drilled through the hearth; fasten to the floor where local code requires.
Masonry chimney

Have it cleaned and inspected first. Fit a UL 1777 type HT (2100°) liner, insulated recommended, not smaller than 6" or 28 square inches. Pass through combustible walls per NFPA 211 (Figure 6-7.5, p. 16).

The chimney must be built to an approved method such as NFPA 211. Have a certified chimney inspector clean and inspect it for code violations, cracks, damaged mortar joints or blockages; a damaged chimney may need re-lining or re-building.

Install a flue liner that meets the type HT (2100°) requirements of UL 1777. Kuma recommends an insulated liner, not smaller than 6" diameter or 28 square inches; any reduction in flue size may cause smoking or poor performance. Double wall connector pipe is recommended.

A pass-through in a combustible wall must be a safe, code-approved method; the manual reprints NFPA 211-2016 Figure 6-7.5 on p. 16 as a diagram.

panels.title: Smoke into the room
items: Bypass not pulled open → open it 1 minute before opening the door
Cold chimney, reverse draft → open a door or window about 5 minutes; restart with small newspaper strips and kindling
Door opened too fast → crack it and let the stove breathe a few seconds
Dirty chimney or cap (screened caps can block in a few weeks) → clean

panels.title: Lazy burn · not hot enough
items: Chimney still cool → allow more time to warm up
Green wood or surface moisture → season about 1 year; cover the pile on top, sides open
Shut down too soon → leave the air open longer
Catalyst plugged with ash → ~20-30 psi air through the baffle grid
Fuel load too small or pieces too large for the coal bed; barometric episodes usually pass within a few days

panels.title: Won't shut down · short burns
items: Door or glass gasket not sealing → check the gaskets (Section 6)
Chimney too tall → check the flue height table
Coal bed too small for the wood → re-kindle; large pieces only on a hot, active bed
Soft wood → harder, denser wood burns longer

panels.title: Catalyst plugged or weak
items: Creosote: wet wood or bypass rod pushed in too soon → burn a hot fire, then soft-brush the face
Soot or fly ash: bypass pushed in too soon, or cardboard, coal, wrapping paper → remove the flame guard (leave the catalyst in place), brush or blow out with dusting air
Lower efficiency: flames on the catalyst from excessive draft → less wood, lower air, or install a damper
Poisoning: don't burn colored paper, cardboard, paneling, painted or treated wood

fire.title: Lighting a fire
fire.html:
Both controls are on the right side of the stove: the bypass control on the upper right, the primary air control on the lower right.

  1. Open the air. Slide the primary air control out, away from the stove, until it stops.
  2. Open the bypass. Give the bypass control a short pull toward you (about ¾") and down. This heats the chimney quickly and keeps smoke out of the room while the door is open.
  3. Build the fire. Open the door and push ash and coals 2" into the firebox. There's an air inlet at the front that must stay clear. Build the fire right on the firebrick, with no grate. For a "top down" fire, put larger pieces on the bottom, smaller pieces above, and kindling on top with a fire starter such as shredded paper.
  4. Light it. You can leave the door slightly cracked to help it start. Close the door once the fire is well lit.
  5. Engage the catalyst. After 15 minutes, or once the catalytic thermometer enters the active range, lift the bypass control. You'll feel it return to the closed position.
  6. Let it settle in. Leave the air open for 20-30 minutes, then slide it in to set the burn rate. Close it down too soon and the fire may go out or the catalyst may stop working.
Never use flammable liquids to start or freshen up a fire. Don't leave the stove unattended with the door open.

firstfire.title: Your first fires
firstfire.html:
Cure the paint slowly

Start your first fire small and increase the heat slowly over a 4 to 5-hour period. The paint cures with heat, and that needs to happen slowly. While it cures, it gives off a smell and sometimes a visible haze. Keep the room well ventilated. The smell fades after a few hours of operation.

Popping and creaking

The metal moves as it heats up and cools down. That makes a normal popping or creaking sound, which will likely decrease after the first several weeks.

Lazy first fires

It's normal for the first few fires to seem a bit lazy. As moisture evaporates from the brick, the fire gets more active. A layer of ash in the bottom of the stove helps keep the coal bed hot. A good thick coal bed and a full load of wood are the keys to the best performance.

The stove is hot while it's running. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; contact may cause skin burns.

burn.title: Setting the burn rate
burn.html:
Once the fire has burned with the air open for 20-30 minutes, slide the primary air control in to set the heat. Slide it out for more heat and in for less. Any position in between works. Approximate burn times:

Low burn · fully closed7-9 hours
Maker's website: Burn Time 9 hours.
Medium burn · about 1/2" open4-6 hours
Start-up or high burn · fully open2-3 hours

Watch the catalytic thermometer

The catalyst is a metal honeycomb that cleans up most of the remaining smoke before it goes up the chimney. Its thermometer shows the right temperature to run the stove at.

  • In the active range (anywhere in the light grey area): normal. Keep it there.
  • Above the range: you're past the catalyst's recommended operating temperature (1300°F). Short periods are fine; slide the air in.
  • Below the range: the stove is getting too cool to work efficiently. Reload before the catalyst goes inactive.
Don't over-fire. Don't leave the air on high for too long. If any part of the stove or chimney glows, shut the air control off right away.

The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory. Federal regulations forbid altering it.

reload.title: Adding more wood
reload.html:
1. Open up. Slide the primary air control fully open and pull the bypass open, just as when you light a fire. Wait 5 minutes so the coals become active and the smoke drafts up the chimney.
  2. Open the door slowly. Crack it a small amount and let the stove "breathe" a few seconds before opening it all the way.
  3. Load. Rake the coals, breaking up any larger pieces. Push ash and coals 2" into the firebox so the front air inlet stays clear. Add wood, then shut the door.
  4. Re-engage the catalyst. Once the catalytic thermometer is in the active range and the wood is well lit, close the bypass.
  5. Let it establish. Leave the air open until the fire is well established, then set your burn rate.
Note: The reload steps on p. 20 say to leave the air open for 10-20 minutes after you reload. A tip on the same page says 20-30 minutes, as do p. 23 and p. 26, and another tip on p. 20 says 10-30 minutes (start-up or reload).

Small hot fires make less creosote than long, low, smoldering fires. Closing the air too soon can cause excessive creosote in the chimney.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Moisture in the wood is the leading cause of creosote build-up in the stove and chimney. This stove is designed to burn natural wood only.

  • Season wood for 1 full year, protected from rain. Wood cut green should sit about 1 year, split and loosely stacked.
  • Moisture content must be 20% or less. Check it with a moisture meter.
  • The recommended wood length is 16".
  • Cover the pile on top but leave the sides open so moving air helps it dry.
  • Air-dried seasoned hardwoods generally burn more efficiently and cleaner than softwoods or green hardwoods. Harder, denser woods also burn longer.

Never burn

Garbage; lawn clippings or yard waste; anything containing rubber (including tires), plastic or asbestos; waste petroleum products, paints, paint thinners or asphalt products; construction or demolition debris; railroad ties or pressure-treated wood; manure or animal remains; salt water driftwood or other salt-water-soaked materials; unseasoned wood; paper products, cardboard, plywood or particleboard.

These can release toxic fumes, make the stove ineffective and cause smoke. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, saw dust, wax and similar substances are still fine.

Burning materials the stove isn't EPA-certified for voids the warranty.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes when they get 3" to 4" deep, and leave 1" of ash in the bottom to help keep a hot charcoal bed.

Make sure the fire is out first. Emptying ashes during an active or full fire will overheat the stove. Always wear gloves when handling hot ashes.

Scoop the ashes out through the loading door, or use the ash drawer if your stove has one:

  1. Turn the ash drawer handle left or right to release the latch.
  2. Pull out the drawer and empty it.
  3. Clean out any ash that fell into the cavity the drawer slides into. Leftover ash can stop the pan from sealing and let too much air reach the fire.
  4. Slide the drawer back, push in to compress the spring and turn the handle down.

Never run the stove with the ash drawer removed or open.

Where the ashes go

Dump them into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid and keep it away from the house. Never use a plastic bucket or paper bag, and never leave ashes near the house or garage.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The stove has an air wash system that keeps the glass clean on its own: on high, the primary air washes the glass as it feeds the fire. Burn the stove on high for 20 to 30 minutes every time you add wood to reduce creosote on the glass. If smoke deposits build up from slow burning, set the air to high for 20 to 30 minutes.

If it still needs cleaning

  • Never clean the glass while it's hot.
  • Use a soft cloth and stove glass cleaner.
  • Don't use steel wool, sandpaper or abrasive cleaners.

Protect it

Closing the door on a piece of wood that's too long will break the glass. Don't strike the glass or slam the door.

If the glass breaks, shut off the primary air control and let the fire burn out. Don't leave the stove unattended, and don't use it again until the glass is replaced. Kuma replacement glass comes with the gasket pre-installed.

care.title: Chimney care & inspections
care.html:
This stove needs periodic inspection and repair to work properly. The manual's checks:

Chimney & connector pipeat least once every two months in the heating season
Catalytic combustorlook at it at least three times a heating season
Door, glass & ash pan gasketsat least once a year
Bricks & ceramic insulationannually

Creosote

Slow fires give off tar and vapors that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. When it ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire that can damage both the chimney and the stove. If creosote has built up, have it removed. Kuma recommends a licensed, professional chimney sweep.

Quick checks

  • Catalyst: pull the flame deflector forward off the baffle. If the catalyst isn't falling apart, crushed or badly warped, it's likely working. If ash plugs it, clean it in place with a soft brush.
  • Gaskets: press with a finger. They should feel somewhat soft; hard, frayed or missing gasket leaks air.
  • Bricks: cracked bricks are fine if they stay in place. Crumbling ones need replacing.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• The stove is hot while it runs. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; contact may cause skin burns.
  • Never use gasoline, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or "freshen up" a fire, and keep them well away from the stove.
  • Don't run the stove with the door open, except cracked open during start-up.
  • Don't operate it with broken glass. Don't strike the glass or slam the door.
  • Always use the baffle boards and ceramic insulation that came with the stove.
  • Smoke detectors and carbon monoxide monitors are recommended in the same room as the stove. A stove that isn't drafting properly can let smoke and carbon monoxide into the home.
  • Keep a type A:B:C fire extinguisher, checked regularly, where everyone in the house knows to find it.
Over-firing: if any part of the stove or chimney glows, the stove is over-firing. Shut the air control off immediately. Over-firing can permanently damage the stove and the catalyst.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Kuma's limited warranty covers the original owner from the date of purchase, for stoves bought from an authorized Kuma dealer. It isn't transferable.

Bricks, gasket, ceramic insulation, paint3 years parts · no labor
Blowers, brick supports, removable wear items5 years parts · 3 years labor
Firebox, burn tubes, legs, glass (thermal breakage), door castingforever parts · 3 years labor
Catalyst6-year structural · 12-year performance

Register within 30 days of purchase at kumastoves.com, or return the registration card from your owner's packet. Parts replaced under warranty get 90-day coverage; parts and accessories bought separately get one year.

Not covered

  • Color changes on the stove's surface, and discoloration of plating or glass
  • Glass shattered by wood impact
  • Noise from the firebox expanding and contracting
  • Damage from incorrect fuel or accelerants, unauthorized changes, or installation that doesn't follow the instructions or local codes
  • Abuse, over-firing, unauthorized repair, improper installation or service
For a claim, contact the dealer where you bought the stove, or Kuma directly. Have your proof of purchase, model name and serial number ready. Shipping and handling aren't covered.

specRating.title: Heat output & emissions
specRating.html:
Heat output12,764 to 29,153 Btu/hr
Maker's website: Cordwood BTU's 63,000 (29,153 EPA est.).
Efficiency78% (High Heating Value)
Particulate emissions1.08 grams per hour
Average CO emissions0.45 grams per minute

Output range is under specific test conditions. Meets the 2020 U.S. EPA crib wood emission limits for wood heaters sold after May 15, 2020. Emissions tested to ASTM E2515 and ASTM E2780 (Report# 0123WM013E); safety tested to UL 1482-2022 (Report # 0123WS011S); tested and listed by OMNI-Test Laboratories Inc., Portland OR.

The text gives one set of figures for Aspen, Tamarack and Aberdeen LE-1. The certification tag on p. 5 is a figure only.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Pipe clearances (A, C, E) are measured to the outside diameter of the pipe; stove clearances (B, D, F) to the stove. Pipe diameter varies by brand, so check that both the stove and the pipe clearances meet the minimums.

Dimensionsingle-wall / double-wall pipe
A (pipe)15" / 9.5"
B (stove)12" / 7"
C (pipe)22" / 21.5"
D (stove)12.5" / 12.5"
E (pipe)15" / 14"
F (stove)5.5" / 5"
L18.5" / 18.5"
N72" / 72"
Alcove (double-wall pipe only)51" wide · 72" tall minimum
Where each letter is measured is shown only in the drawing on this page, which also carries the callout 18" or follow pipe manufacturer's instructions. Read these values with the drawing.

The text gives one clearance table for all three models. These clearances may be reduced only by approved methods in NFPA 211. Always follow local building codes.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
Floor protection must be non-combustible, go underneath the stove and extend to the sides and front.

Sides (G) · measured to the top plate6"
Front (H) · measured to the stove face16"
TypeType 1 (ember protection) · no insulation R-value required
Through-wall installationsunderneath and 2" to either side of the horizontal connector pipe

The layout is shown in the figure on this page.

specFlue.title: Chimney & connector pipe
specFlue.html:
ChimneyUL-103HT factory-built all-fuel, or lined masonry to NFPA 211
Minimum diameter6"
Masonry linerUL 1777, type HT (2100°); not smaller than 6" or 28 square inches
Connector24ga. single wall black stove pipe or listed double wall connector pipe
Fastening3 screws per pipe joint, including 3 at the stove

Kuma recommends double wall connector pipe for better draft and less creosote; it's required in mobile homes and alcoves. Single wall pipe may only connect the stove to an approved masonry or stainless steel chimney, never as a chimney, exterior, or through a wall or ceiling. Depending on the double wall pipe, it may also need fastening at the chimney.

Don't connect to a chimney flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution or duct system. No field-fabricated or makeshift parts.

specHeight.title: Chimney height
specHeight.html:
Minimum flue height recommendations:

No offsets in the chimney14 ft
30° or 45° offsets15 ft
90° offsets16 ft
90° offsets with 2-3 feet of horizontal run20 ft
90° offsets into exterior chimney22 ft

The chimney must exit the roof by at least 3 feet and be at least 2 feet higher than any part of the roof within 10 feet. The venting system (chimney + connector pipe) should be at least 14 feet from the stove top to the venting cap.

A chimney that is too short reduces draft; one that is too tall increases it, and the troubleshooting chart lists a too-tall chimney as a cause of a stove that won't shut down.

specModels.title: Models & dimensional drawings
specModels.html:
Aspen LE-1, Tamarack LE-1 and Aberdeen LE-1 are all Model K-181 and share this manual. The text gives one set of ratings, clearances, floor protection and chimney rules for all three. It tells them apart only with separate dimensional drawings:

Tamarack LE-1p. 6
Aspen LE-1p. 7
Aberdeen LE-1p. 8

The drawings are figures (all dimensions in inches), so no heights, widths, depths or weights appear in the text. Take them from the drawing for the model you're installing.

The 125 CFM variable speed blower (KA-BL-05) fits Aspen, Tamarack and Aberdeen. The ash pan kit and blower are optional; legs or a pedestal kit go on during assembly.

specMobile.title: Mobile home installation
specMobile.html:
• An outside air kit (KA OA 1) is required for all mobile home installations. Follow the instructions in its box.
  • Double wall connector pipe is required; single wall pipe may not be used as a connector in mobile homes.
  • Drill through the hearth and connect the stove to the metal frame underneath the home with 8-gauge ground wire and appropriate connectors.
  • Fasten the stove to the floor when local code requires it.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of the floor, wall and ceiling/roof. Never install in a sleeping room.

The "Intake air requirements" heading on p. 12 has no text; any further outside-air detail there is in the figure.

specCatalyst.title: Catalytic combustor
specCatalyst.html:
CombustorApplied Catalysts ACI-5M, Long Life
Kuma part #KR-CT-01 (includes gasket KR-GK-01)
Recommended operating temperature1300°F; above the active range you exceed it
Working temperaturetypically in excess of 500°F, often in excess of 1,000°F
Visual inspectionat least three times during the heating season
Cleaningsoft brush, or ~20-30 psi air through the cells

Below 500°F, see the catalyst troubleshooting chart. Smoke check: compare chimney smoke with the exhaust routed through the catalyst and with the bypass open; significantly more smoke shows in bypass mode.

Replacing the catalyst

Pull the flame guard forward off the baffle, pull the catalyst out by its 2 handles, and clear old gasket from the baffle cavity. Slide the new one in until it stops (leave its tape and stretch film on). Wrap any gap larger than 1/8" with extra gasket; it expands 2-3 times its original thickness once heated.

Burn tubes & baffle insulation

Burn tubes unbolt with a 7/16" wrench; pull right, then down and out. To replace the ceramic insulation, remove the 3 burn tubes so the baffle comes down, note their order, and align the blanket's cut-out with the bypass opening. Then re-install the baffle and the 3 burn tubes.

The manual also prints "the 4 burn tubes" in the re-install step on p. 27; the same paragraph says to remove the 3 burn tubes, and the parts list on p. 30 shows three (front, middle, rear).
Tamper warning: operating the stove with the catalytic element deactivated or removed is against federal regulations.

review.notes: Model distinction: the manual covers Aspen LE-1, Tamarack LE-1 and Aberdeen LE-1 as one Model K-181 with a single set of text specs; it tells them apart only by separate dimensional drawings (Tamarack p. 6, Aspen p. 7, Aberdeen p. 8) that have no extractable text. So no per-model numeric rows were possible; the guide gives a per-model row pointing to each drawing page. Catalog height, width, depth, weight, firebox volume, heating area and cordwood output do not appear in the manual text and could not be checked; every other checkable catalog spec (heat output range, 78% HHV, 1.08 g/hr, EPA 2020, 6" flue, 16" wood, hybrid combustion, 7-9 hour low burn, 125 CFM blower, KA OA 1 outside air, mobile home approval, clearance and floor-protection values) matches. Figures only: certification tag (p. 5), dimensional drawings (pp. 6-8), clearance drawing (p. 9), floor protection layout (p. 11), typical installation (p. 14), NFPA 211 wall pass-through (p. 16), lighting and cut-away illustrations (pp. 18-23), parts diagrams (pp. 28-29). The 'Intake air requirements' heading (p. 12) has no text under it. Clearances (p. 9): values transcribed from the text table with their letters; the text defines only A/C/E as pipe and B/D/F as stove clearances. Where each letter applies, and what L, N and the 18" or follow pipe manufacturer's instructions callout measure, is drawing-only, so the catalog's back-wall/side-wall labels for A-F cannot be confirmed from the text (numbers match). Chimney inspection: p. 25 says at least once every two months in the heating season; the troubleshooting chart (pp. 31-32) says checked and cleaned if necessary every few months. The guide uses p. 25's interval. The troubleshooting draft example cites an 8" chimney (pp. 31, 32) and a 6" chimney (p. 31); the example is not used. Reload step 1 says wait 5 minutes with the bypass open (p. 20); troubleshooting says open the bypass 1 minute before opening the door (p. 31). Both shown, as written; read as compatible. The flame part is called flame diffuser (p. 11), flame deflector (p. 26) and flame guard (pp. 26, 30, 32). The manual has no blower electrical rating or operating instructions and no weights. No French or scrambled text.
